specAnchors.text: understand why gravitational field strength, g , varies and know that it is different on other planets and the Moon from that on the Earth

primer.text: Weight is the gravitational pull on an object, and how hard that pull is per kilogram — the field strength g — changes from world to world. A planet's greater mass means stronger gravity: Earth offers about 10 N/kg, the Moon less, the gas giants more, while the object's mass itself never changes.

modules.title: Gravitational field strength and weight
modules.opening: Weight is the gravitational pull acting on an object, and it depends on the local gravitational field strength g. A more massive planet pulls harder: g is about 10 N/kg on Earth, smaller on the Moon, and larger on the gas giants — so the same object weighs different amounts on different worlds while its mass stays the same.
keyPoints: Weight is the gravitational pull acting on an object.
The greater a planet's mass, the greater its gravitational field strength.
On Earth's surface g is about 10 N/kg; the Moon's is less, the gas giants' more.
An object's mass is the same everywhere, but its weight changes with the field.
Weight is what keeps objects on the ground and satellites in orbit.

low.restatement: Same object, different worlds: mass fixed, weight tracks the local g.
low.analogy: The same shopping bag feels heavier when someone helps you lift it less — the bag never changed, the pull did.
low.examPointer: Mass in kg never travels; weight in N goes wherever the field sends it.

medium.restatement: g is per-kilogram pull: roughly 10 N/kg on Earth, below it on the Moon, above it on the gas giants, scaling with planetary mass.
medium.analogy: A stronger magnet under the same iron filings: the filings (mass) are identical, the grip (field) is not.
medium.examPointer: Exam questions supply Earth's g — use it, and never quote g for other worlds from memory.

glossary.definition: The gravitational pull acting on an object.
The gravitational pull per kilogram, about 10 N/kg on Earth, varying between worlds.
The amount of matter in an object; unchanged from world to world.
